editorial_contributions.text:
The inequalities are these: for every cspc (= centrally symmetric plane convex) body \(K\) 
\[
 \theta_L(K) - 1 \geq 1-\delta_L(K),\quad \theta_L(K)-1\leq 1.25\sqrt{1-\delta_L(K)}, 
\]
 where \(\theta_L(K)\) and \(\delta_L(K)\) are the densities of the thinnest covering and densest packing of the plane with lattice translates of \(K\). Furthermore in these inequalities the order of magnitude cannot be improved: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist cspc bodies \(K_\varepsilon\) and \(M_\varepsilon\) such that 
\[
 \theta_L(K_\varepsilon)-1<(1+\varepsilon)(1-\delta_L(K_\varepsilon)) \quad \text{and} \quad \theta_L(M_\varepsilon)-1>(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{1-\delta_L(M_\varepsilon)}. 
\]
 The proofs depend on the author's exact description of the set of all points \((x,y)\) with the property that there exists \(K \in P_8\) (the family of all cspc octagons) such that \( \theta_L(K)=x, \delta_L(K)=y\). 


The paper begins with a brief description of the concepts involved and known results with adequate references. It ends with a half dozen open problems.

Summary: In 2012, \textit{Lenny Jones} [Integers 12, No. 4, 659--667, A11 (2012; Zbl 1262.11018)] proved that there are infinitely many positive integers that cannot be expressed as \(F_n - p\) or \(F_n + p\), where \(F_n\) is the \(n\)th term of the Fibonacci sequence and \(p\) denotes a prime. The smallest integer with this property he could find has 950 digits.

 We prove that the numbers 135225 and 208641 have this property as well. We also show that there are infinitely many integers that cannot be written as \(\pm F_n \pm p\), for any choice of the signs. In particular, 64369395 is such a number. We answer a question of Jones by showing that there exist infinitely many integers \(k\) such that neither \(k\) nor \(k + 1\) can be written as \(F_n \pm p\). Finally, we prove that there exist infinitely many perfect squares and infinitely many perfect cubes that cannot be written as \(F_n \pm p\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: Ausgehend von einem gegebenen konvexen Polygon \(P\) mit \(n\) Ecken in der Ebene betrachtet man folgendes Problem: Man finde das flächengrösste konvexe Polygon \(Q\) mit \(m\) Ecken, das ganz in \(P\) liegt. Wie klein kann dann der Quotient der Flächeninhalte \(\Delta(Q)/\Delta(P)\) sein? Formal lässt sich diese Frage in folgende Formel kleiden:
\[
f_n(m)=\min_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n} \max_{Q \subset P,|Q|=m} \frac{\Delta(Q)}{\Delta(P)}\;.
\]
Dabei wird das Maximum über alle in \(P\) enthaltenen Polygone \(Q\) mit \(m\) Ecken, und das Minimum über alle konvexen Polygone \(P\) mit \(n\) Ecken genommen. Die betrachtete Frage spielt in der Robotik eine Rolle. Die Werte \(f_4(3), f_5(4)\) und \(f_6(3)\) sind bekannt. In der vorliegenden Arbeit werden nun \(f_5(3), f_6(5)\) und \(f_6(4)\) berechnet und Schranken für \(f_n(n-1)\) angegeben. Zudem werden die bekannten Schranken für \(f_n(m)\) verbessert.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k\) with the property that \(k \cdot 2^{n} + 1\) is composite for all positive integer values of \(n\). A Riesel number is defined similarly; the only difference is that \(k \cdot 2^{n} - 1\) is composite for all positive integer values of \(n\). In this paper we find Sierpiński and Riesel numbers among the terms of the well-known Fibonacci sequence. These numbers are smaller than all previously constructed examples. We also find a 23-digit number which is simultaneously a Sierpiński and a Riesel number. This improves on the current record established by Filaseta, Finch and Kozek in 2008 [\textit{M. Filaseta} et al., J. Number Theory 128, No. 7, 1916--1940 (2008; Zbl 1221.11003)]. Finally, we prove that there are infinitely many values of \(n\) such that the Fibonacci numbers \(F_{n}\) and \(F_{n+1}\) are both Sierpiński numbers.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper under review considers packing of infinite cylinders in \(3\)-dimensional Euclidean space. 

It is known that densest such packing is achieved by a collection of parallel cylinders, whose perpendicular \(2\)-dimensional section is a hexagonal circle packing in the plane; this density is \(\pi/\sqrt{12} = 0.9068\dots\) [\textit{A. Bezdek} and \textit{W. Kuperberg}, Mathematika 37, No. 1, 74--80 (1990; Zbl 0715.52006)]. This result raises a natural question: how a dense can a packing of nonparallel cylinders be? Nonparallel cylinder packings with density \(\pi^2/576 = 0.017\dots\) were constructed in [\textit{K. Kuperberg}, Mathematika 37, No. 2, 324--331 (1990; Zbl 0721.52012)], and a refined construction with density \(5/12 = 0.4166\dots\) was given in [\textit{C. Graf} and \textit{P. Paukowitsch}, Elem. Math. 52, No. 2, 71--83 (1997; Zbl 0904.52008)]. 

In the current paper, the authors produce such a construction with density \(1/2\). Moreover, they show that there exist packings in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with no two cylinders parallel, whose local density is arbitrarily close to the local density of a packing with parallel cylinders.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: More than thirty years ago, Paul Erdős asked the following question:

Does there exist an absolute constant \(c\) such that any measurable planar region \(R\) of area \(c\) contains the vertices of a unit-area triangle?

In traditional Erdős style, the question stood the test of time and despite the efforts of many mathematicians it is still wide open. We give a positive answer with \(c=4\ln 2\) in two particular cases:

Case 1: there exists a direction \(l\) such that the projection of \(R\) onto \(l\) is an interval.

Case 2: there exists a direction \(l\) such that the projection of \(R\) onto \(l\) is the union of \(n\) disjoint intervals, where \(n\) is the number of connected components of \(R\).

These results suggest that the answer to the general question is affirmative.

title.title: Shifting Lucas sequences away from primes

editorial_contributions.text:
Given \(K = A_1A_2 \dots A_n\), a convex polygon with \(n \geq 5\) vertices, the authors draw the short diagonals \(A_1A_3, A_2A_4, \dots, A_{n-2}A_n, A_{n-1}A_1\), and \(A_nA_2\). A new convex \(n\)-gon \(K_1 = B_1B_2 \dots B_n\) is created inside \(K\), where \(B_i\) is the intersection point of \(A_{i-1}A_{i+1}\) and \(A_iA_{i+2}\) for all \(1 \leq i \leq n\).

This construction was introduced by \textit{R. Schwartz} [Exp. Math. 1, No. 1, 71--81 (1992; Zbl 0765.52004)]. It is known as the pentagram map.

Let \(K\) be a polygon and let \(\Delta(K)\) be its area. Then, for every integer \(n \geq 5\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a convex \(n\)-gon \(K\) such that \(\Delta(K_1)/\Delta(K) < \varepsilon\) and, for every integer \(n \geq 6\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a convex \(n\)-gon \(K\) such that \(\Delta(K_1)/\Delta(K) > 1 - \varepsilon\).

When \(K\) is a pentagon it is not known how large the ratio \(\Delta(K_1)/\Delta(K)\) is.

The authors show: Let \(K\) be a convex pentagon and let \(K_1\) be the pentagon formed by the diagonals of \(K\). Then \(\Delta(K_1)/ \Delta(K) \leq (7- 3\sqrt{5})/2\) with equality if and only if \(K\) is an affine regular pentagon.

They give a description of prior attempts to solve the problem, they compute \(\Delta(K_1)\) and they make a generalization attempt.

title.title: On the area of the polygon determined by the short diagonals of a convex polygon

editorial_contributions.text:
The distance count of a point in a finite pointset is defined as the number of distinct distances from this point to other points of the pointset. So \(n\) equidistant points on a line have distance counts ranging from \(\lfloor{1\over 2}n\rfloor\) in the middle to \(n-1\) at the ends. Erdős and Fishburn asked for the maximum number \(D_d(n)\) of distinct distance counts that can occur among \(n\) points in \(d\)-dimensional euclidean space, and their asymptotic rates \(\lambda_d:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}{D_d(n)\over n}\). Trivially \({1\over 2}\leq\lambda_d\leq 1\), since \(D_d(n)\leq n-1\). The authors give constructions that show \(\lambda_2\geq 0.7\), \(\lambda_3\geq 0.833\), \(\lambda_4\geq 0.875\), and \(\lambda_d\geq 1-{2\over d}\). They also give some upper bounds on \(D_d(n)\) and determine some exact values.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0868.00054].
